claims.text: Adding approximately 3 at.% boron to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy enhances its glass-forming ability.
Adding approximately 3 at.% boron improves the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The baseline material is a rapidly cooled, amorphous, phosphorus-containing high-entropy alloy without boron.
The proposed intervention is the addition of approximately 3 at.% boron.
A boron range of roughly 2–5 at.% is optimal for the proposed effect.
Keeping boron within roughly 2–5 at.% avoids formation of crystalline boride phases.
The beneficial effect requires rapid cooling conditions that normally yield a glassy state.
Boron addition increases atomic packing density.
Boron addition increases the formation of icosahedral short-range-order clusters.
The small size of boron as a metalloid enables it to refine the alloy's local atomic structure by promoting denser packing.
Denser local atomic packing reduces free volume.
Reduced free volume and stabilization of icosahedral clusters hinder crystallization kinetics.
Hindered crystallization kinetics produce improved glass-forming ability and a higher crystallization onset temperature.
The boron-modified alloy should have a larger critical casting thickness than the boron-free baseline.
The boron-modified alloy should have a higher DSC crystallization onset temperature than the boron-free baseline.
Cooling that is too slow should eliminate the anticipated improvement.
Boron content above the optimum may cause boride formation and eliminate the anticipated improvement.
Failure to obtain statistically significant increases in both critical casting thickness and crystallization onset temperature, or detection of crystalline borides, would falsify the hypothesis.
